item.description: Insider buying and federal contract awards gave no tradeable edge. Inventory build predicts semiconductor gross margins, but barely moves returns.
item.content:encoded:
AltAlpha is a research platform for testing whether free, public alternative data predicts company fundamentals and stock returns. It turns SEC filings and market data into point-in-time features: every value carries the moment it became public, not the date of the event it describes. I wanted to know which free datasets can be tested honestly, and whether any of them still carries an edge.

How it works #

It started with a survey of what free data a script can reach. Most of the classic alternative datasets (job postings, web traffic, app downloads, satellite and shipping data) are paid. The free ones with company-level history and clean timestamps are insider filings, federal contract awards, Wikipedia page views and Taiwanese supplier revenue. I ranked five hypotheses by data availability and testability, and have tested three so far.

Everything hangs off EDGAR, which stamps each filing with its acceptance time to the second. The store holds 3.49 million insider open-market trades since 2006, 440,233 XBRL filings since 2009 (XBRL is the machine-readable tagging in SEC financial statements) and 417,257 earnings-release 8-Ks. A unit test checks that a 10-K accepted five minutes after a cut-off stays invisible until the next month.

Each study fixes its main tests in code before the first run. Every other variant is logged as a trial and goes into a multiple-testing correction (Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg). Backtests charge spreads, square-root market impact and borrow fees, and are re-run at sizes from $1m to $1bn.

What I found #

Study Question Result
Insider purchases Do unusual buys by officers and directors predict earnings and returns? No. All three pre-registered tests fail; 3 of 150 variants survive correction
Inventory build Does inventory growing faster than sales predict margins and returns? Margins strongly; returns only weakly
Federal contracts Do contract awards predict contractor revenue and returns? No. Nothing beyond the company’s own revenue trend

Insider buying is priced within a day. A purchase filing moves the stock +1.2–1.3% on the trading day it becomes public, both in the focus industries (semiconductors, AI infrastructure and defence) and in the broad market. Across the broad market, routine purchases get +0.45% and sales −0.16%. Little is left after that: a month-end portfolio of recent buyers beat its universe by 2.8% a year (t 0.54).

Inventory build predicts gross margins. One standard deviation more build means 1.15 percentage points less gross-margin change next quarter (t −3.3), and the highest- and lowest-build fifths end up 6.7 points apart. The test includes firms that later disappeared and replicates in the rest of the market. The return spread, 8.0% a year (t 1.95), falls just short of significance, and the investable version nets a Sharpe ratio of only 0.37.

Contract awards add nothing. I attributed $2.76tn of USAspending obligations to 29 listed contractors through the parent entity recorded on each action, because the site’s name search returns today’s names for old contracts. Awards correlate with next-quarter revenue growth, but the effect vanishes once current growth is controlled (t −0.09). Ignoring publication lags would have inflated that correlation from 0.12 to 0.17.

A live margin screen #

The inventory result now runs as a live screen of semiconductor and AI-hardware filers, fed by the SEC’s XBRL API within hours of each filing. On 17 November 2026 it scored 107 of 160 companies and listed every exclusion with a reason. Over 52 out-of-sample quarters, the best-forecast fifth beat the worst by 9.5 points of realised margin change (t 10.2). Most of that comes from the margin trend, not from inventory. Build works as a warning, but only where sales are falling or growing by less than 30%.

Limits #

  • Free daily prices cover only companies still listed, so every return test is survivorship-biased; the fundamental tests are not. In the insider study, 1,977 of 4,817 purchase events fall in firms with no price data.
  • There are no historical analyst estimates, so an earnings surprise is measured against the same quarter a year earlier.
  • Without intraday data, the filing-day reaction cannot be tested at the hour level.

How it’s built #

Python, with parquet tables and a DuckDB catalogue as the point-in-time store, statsmodels for the regressions, and scikit-learn and LightGBM for walk-forward models.

item.title: A browser editor for game-theory trees, with LaTeX and image export
item.description: Draw extensive-form game trees with chance moves, information sets and payoffs, then export them as PNG, SVG or TikZ. Nothing to install and no account.
item.content:encoded:
Game Tree Studio is a single-page editor for the trees used in game theory. An extensive-form game is a game drawn as a tree: each branch point is a move by a player or by chance, and the leaves hold the payoffs. It is the standard way to show who moves when and what they know. Drawing one neatly by hand or in LaTeX is slow, so this editor makes it a matter of clicks and keystrokes, then exports the result for papers, slides and course work.

What it does #

  • Quick tree building. Double-click a node to add moves, press 1 to 6 to give it to a player, or N to make it a chance node.
  • Information sets (nodes a player cannot tell apart). Shift-click them and press I. They are drawn as a dashed line, a dotted line or an oval, and the move labels stay in sync across the set.
  • Chance moves with numeric or symbolic probabilities, such as 1/3 or 1 − π. The editor warns when numeric probabilities don’t add up to 1.
  • Payoffs as expressions, with a small LaTeX-like markup for subscripts, superscripts, Greek letters and true minus signs.
  • Continua of actions, drawn as an arc between the extreme choices, with one representative move and a range label.
  • Highlighted moves, a thick line with an arrow, to mark a strategy profile or a path found by backward induction (solving the game from the leaves back to the root).
  • Layout and notation options: top-to-bottom or left-to-right trees, spacing sliders, terminal nodes on one row, three payoff styles, round or square chance nodes, serif or sans-serif text and optional colours by player.
  • Undo and redo, copy and paste of subtrees, keyboard navigation, light and dark themes, and a layout that works on phones.

Export #

  • PNG at three times screen resolution, for documents, slides and course submissions.
  • SVG for the web or further editing, or a copy straight to the clipboard.
  • TikZ for LaTeX, with every element at the coordinates shown in the editor and simple fractions typeset as fractions.
  • GTDraw .ef files, for fine-tuning the typesetting in that tool.
  • JSON, the editor’s own format. Dragging a saved file onto the canvas opens the game again.

How it’s built #

One HTML page, one stylesheet and one JavaScript file that holds the tree model, the layout, the SVG rendering and every exporter. There is no build step, no server and no account. The live copy runs on GitHub Pages, and the code is MIT-licensed.

Limits #

  • It draws games; it doesn’t solve them. Highlighted paths are marked by hand.
  • Storage is per browser and per address. Games are kept in the browser’s local storage, so a copy on GitHub Pages and a copy opened from disk keep separate libraries, and clearing site data removes them. Saving a game file keeps a copy that opens anywhere.

item.title: AAOI alt-data tracker
item.description: Seven public data series on Applied Optoelectronics and its market, refreshed weekly into tidy files and a model-ready workbook.
item.content:encoded:
One command collects seven public data series on Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) and the market around it, appends anything new to tidy CSV files and rebuilds an Excel workbook that links straight into a valuation model.

The sources include SEC filings, US Census trade data, tariff-code lookups, job postings and Texas construction-project filings for the company’s new fabs, plus a few hand-maintained inputs.

The ground rules are built into the code:

  • official APIs first, and every host’s robots.txt checked on every run;
  • no logins, paywalls, CAPTCHAs or rate-limit workarounds;
  • nothing invented, interpolated or estimated: a missing input leaves a blank and a logged reason;
  • every raw response cached with its retrieval time.

item.title: A chess trainer built from my blunders in over 12,000 online games
item.description: Stockfish checked every move of my online games against my opponents’ moves in the same games, then 1,212 of the positions became a browser trainer with spaced repetition.
item.content:encoded:
I have played more than 12,000 online chess games since 2018, and my results match my rating. So the useful question is not whether I make mistakes, but which mistakes I make more often than the players I meet. This project answers that with an engine review of every game, then turns the answers into a trainer.

How the review works #

  • Data. 12,217 games from the chess.com and lichess public APIs, from September 2018 to October 2026. Stockfish 19 checked every move of the 11,907 standard-chess games: 819,411 positions.
  • The baseline is my opponents. Every comparison is me against my opponents in the same games: players at my rating, at the same time controls, in the same kinds of positions. That separates real leaks from noise in a way that comparing with an engine cannot.
  • Calibrated engine budgets. 20,000 to 60,000 nodes a position, depending on the time control, chosen after a 30-game calibration against a one-million-node reference. Blunder flags matched the reference with precision 0.91 and recall 0.85-0.88.
  • Checked scoring. Win% and the blunder threshold (a drop of 15 Win% points) follow lichess’s formulas. On 425 games, my Win% correlates at 0.991 with lichess’s own server analysis.
  • A second pass. All 50,158 blitz and rapid blunders were searched again for full lines and tagged with a tactical motif such as a fork, pin, skewer or back-rank mate. Every example was re-verified at 1.5 million nodes, and 510 of 516 held up.

What it found #

  • I walk into tactics more often than my opponents, mostly in level blitz middlegames. Over the last 12 months of blitz (2,054 games), my moves allowed pins 84% more often than theirs, skewers 74% more often and knight forks 39% more often. It isn’t time trouble: in 92% of the blitz games I lost to a single blunder, I still had more than a fifth of my clock.
  • I play rapid too fast. I reach move 40 with two-thirds of my clock left, against my opponents’ half, and 21% of my moves take under a second (theirs: 7%). In blitz the same speed is a weapon: opponents lose on time to me 4.6 times per 100 games, and I lose on time to them 1.6 times.
  • Four opening spots cost points, each confirmed by a deeper engine check.
  • Strengths to keep: converting won positions, endgames, defending bad positions and not tilting after losses.

The trainer #

A static web page drills 1,212 positions from my own games, weighted towards the patterns the review flagged. The engine graded every legal move in each position, so any move that holds counts as right, not just the engine’s first choice. There are six drills:

  • Spot the threat: play the reply that punishes the move I actually played.
  • Find a safe move in the position before the blunder.
  • Safe or blunder?: a quick judgement of a candidate move.
  • Missed shots: find the punishment for an opponent’s mistake I let go.
  • Opening fixes: repeated opening positions where my usual move scores badly.
  • Daily mix of the above, due reviews first.

Spaced repetition brings a solved position back after 1, 3, 7, 16, 35 and then 75 days, and a missed one within about ten minutes. An optional clock adds blitz-style time limits, and progress is saved in the browser. The review also produced three study files of my own positions for lichess.

Limits #

  • The motif labels are heuristic, modelled on lichess puzzle themes and checked by eye on about 60 positions. Both sides get the same labeller, so the gaps are more reliable than the raw counts.
  • Opponents change from game to game, so the comparison is with the average player I meet.
  • Patterns such as “fast moves blunder more” are associations, not proof of cause.

How it’s built #

A chain of Python scripts fetches the games, normalises them, runs Stockfish on every position, extracts features, re-checks the blunders, tags motifs, computes the metrics and draws the charts, saving every table as CSV. The trainer is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no server.

item.title: GTA VI sentiment model
item.description: Google Trends, Reddit and Wikipedia data turned into a launch forecast and a valuation for Take-Two.
item.content:encoded:
How much can online attention say about the biggest game launch in years, and does it matter for the stock?

  • Search: Google Trends interest, chained across five-year windows, puts GTA VI’s share of searches in the weeks before launch level with GTA V’s before its 2013 release.
  • Purchase intent: Reddit comments classified by whether people say they are buying. The “buying” share rose from 61% at the price reveal to 71% in October.
  • Cross-checks: traffic-adjusted Wikipedia pageviews and reported digital pre-order counts.

Those feed a sales projection of about 38 million copies by March 2027 (range 28–48 million) and a discounted-cash-flow model of Take-Two. The launch hardly moves intrinsic value: the probability-weighted value is $124 a share against a $195 price, and the swing factor is GTA VI Online, which has not launched yet.
